frictionVectors.title: EU Gas Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian pipeline gas and LNG, giving Algiers bargaining power while exposing it to demand shifts, pricing pressure, and regulatory disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Instability
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya complicates border control and threatens energy corridors, while Algeria resists deeper external military involvement.

frictionVectors.title: External Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting U.S., European, Chinese, and Gulf interest because of its access to Central African copper and cobalt, creating leverage over Angola's transport strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Oil Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues remain central to fiscal stability, while legacy Chinese financing and foreign operators limit policy flexibility despite efforts to expand domestic participation.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Pipeline Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Niger have disrupted the operating environment around the Niger-Benin oil export route, threatening transit revenues and exposing Benin's infrastructure to regional politics.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea Security
frictionVectors.details: Benin is strengthening maritime and border security as illicit trafficking and militant spillover from the Sahel threaten the Cotonou logistics hub.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond Market Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains strong leverage through diamond governance and local beneficiation, but remains exposed to global price weakness and the bargaining power of major trading partners.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Infrastructure Gap
frictionVectors.details: Interest in copper, nickel, and other critical minerals is rising, yet limited rail, water, and power infrastructure could increase reliance on external investors.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Alignment
frictionVectors.details: The junta's expanding security relationship with Russia reduces Western influence but creates new dependence on external military assistance and opaque political commitments.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Control
frictionVectors.details: Efforts to increase state participation, local processing, and oversight of artisanal mining aim to retain more gold value domestically, but insecurity and informal networks constrain implementation.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Governance and Informal Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Gold and strategic mineral production remain vulnerable to opaque licensing, informal exports, and limited state oversight. External traders and regional networks capture significant value relative to domestic institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security and Trade Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained, complicating border security and commercial transit. Burundi's dependence on regional corridors leaves its sovereignty exposed to diplomatic and infrastructure pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed investment in ports, logistics, and digital connectivity strengthens Cabo Verde's strategic value but increases dependence on external capital and security partners. Competition among European, Chinese, and transatlantic actors is likely to remain visible.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Energy Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains highly exposed to tourism flows, imported fuel, and climate stress. External financing supports resilience, but fiscal and infrastructure choices are constrained by dependence on donors and foreign investors.

highlights: Ports and Energy Assets Attract Rivalry

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure and Resource Access
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain important in roads, hydropower, and extractive-linked infrastructure, providing capacity while deepening repayment and strategic dependence. The state has limited leverage to ensure that major projects generate broad domestic value.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict and Corridor Security
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest continues to threaten transport, agriculture, and energy assets. Instability also complicates the use of Cameroon as a regional transit and export corridor.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian security personnel and political support has expanded external influence over strategic decision-making. Mining access and security arrangements remain opaque, limiting transparent state control over resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor Dependence and Armed-Group Disruption
frictionVectors.details: Landlocked trade depends heavily on vulnerable routes through Cameroon and neighboring states. Armed groups, weak logistics, and limited administrative reach constrain the government's ability to secure extraction zones and collect revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Infrastructure and Revenue Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains central to public finance and external bargaining, leaving the state exposed to price volatility and the priorities of foreign operators. Pipeline and export infrastructure provide revenue but do not eliminate deep regional and fiscal vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Spillover and External Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: The war in Sudan is intensifying refugee, border-security, and humanitarian pressures in eastern Chad. As France recalibrates its military presence and other partners seek influence, N'Djamena is balancing sovereignty claims against urgent security dependence.

frictionVectors.title: France–Comoros Territorial Tensions
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved status of Mayotte limits Comoros’ control over surrounding maritime space and sustains dependence on French security and economic links.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gulf, French, and other external partners influence infrastructure and development priorities amid limited domestic fiscal capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt assets remain central to competition among Chinese, Western, and regional investors, while weak state oversight limits Kinshasa’s bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda–M23 Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east undermines territorial sovereignty, disrupts mineral governance, and sustains accusations of external support for armed networks.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: State revenues and external bargaining power remain heavily tied to offshore oil, leaving national finances exposed to price shifts and foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-funded roads, rail, and energy projects expand connectivity but may constrain policy autonomy through financing and repayment obligations.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa Sovereignty Gap
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan is strengthening domestic processing and price management, but global buyers and external finance still capture substantial value from the cocoa economy.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Sahel Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability across Burkina Faso and Mali place pressure on northern borders, security spending, and transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Base Competition
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position near Bab el-Mandeb through multiple foreign military facilities, but this dependence can narrow strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked port and rail infrastructure has increased connectivity while raising concerns over debt concentration, revenue control, and vulnerability to regional disruptions.

highlights: Suez Canal remains a strategic revenue lifeline
Gulf and IMF financing deepen external leverage

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian control over Nile flows and seeks a binding operating agreement for the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. The dispute remains tied to wider Red Sea and Gulf rivalries.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-financed strategic assets
frictionVectors.details: IMF conditions and Gulf investment provide critical liquidity but increase foreign influence over ports, real estate, and state-linked enterprises. Suez revenues remain vulnerable to regional shipping disruption.

highlights: Hydrocarbon decline is compressing state revenues
China remains central to infrastructure and finance

frictionVectors.title: Maturing oil and gas fields
frictionVectors.details: Falling hydrocarbon output limits fiscal space and heightens pressure to attract foreign operators into offshore projects. The state retains formal control but remains dependent on external capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: China-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese contractors and lenders remain important for roads, ports, and public works. Weak transparency and concentrated political control reduce bargaining leverage over project terms.

highlights: Red Sea location amplifies strategic leverage

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to Yemen make it strategically valuable as shipping security deteriorates. Competition among Gulf states, Turkey, and Western powers creates pressure for access while Asmara resists formal alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque mining partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide hard-currency income but depend on foreign firms and remain politically opaque. Sanctions exposure and labor-rights concerns constrain broader investment options.

highlights: South African trade corridors remain indispensable
Sugar and apparel exports face external market pressure

frictionVectors.title: South African economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South Africa for imports, transport access, electricity, and regional finance. This limits strategic autonomy while Pretoria remains the principal stabilizing economic partner.

frictionVectors.title: Textile preference uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Apparel exports remain exposed to changes in preferential access to United States and regional markets. Labor and governance concerns can quickly translate into lost orders or investment.

highlights: Debt restructuring and regional conflict constrain autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Nile diplomacy confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam expands Ethiopia's electricity potential and bargaining power, but Egypt and Sudan continue to demand predictable water-release rules. The issue remains a major source of regional diplomatic friction.

frictionVectors.title: External finance and conflict exposure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, IMF engagement, and foreign investment are needed to stabilize the economy, giving creditors and partners greater policy leverage. Insecurity in several regions continues to threaten transport, energy, and industrial infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: French commercial influence
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater Gabonese control over oil, mining, and strategic infrastructure while managing longstanding French corporate and political influence.

frictionVectors.title: Processing and logistics bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Gabon retains strong manganese and petroleum assets, but limited domestic processing capacity and dependence on rail and port infrastructure constrain value capture.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on foreign aid, remittances, tourism, and regional security support, limiting autonomous control over strategic economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal fishing and maritime enforcement
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fleets and weak monitoring threaten coastal fisheries, creating persistent sovereignty concerns and revenue losses for local communities.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector leakage
frictionVectors.details: Gold remains Ghana's strongest external-earnings asset, but illicit mining, foreign trading networks, and environmental damage reduce state capture of the sector's full value.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-supported stabilization narrow fiscal room, while offshore oil and emerging lithium projects require careful management to avoid renewed dependency.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mining corridors
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Western, and other foreign-led consortia dominate capital-intensive bauxite and iron-ore development, leaving Guinea dependent on external finance, technology, and export routes.

frictionVectors.title: Junta and contract uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: The military government's resource-nationalist posture has increased demands for local content and infrastructure, but political uncertainty and opaque renegotiations complicate sovereign oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain capture
frictionVectors.details: The economy depends heavily on raw cashew exports, with foreign traders and processors capturing much of the value while domestic processing remains limited.

frictionVectors.title: Illicit maritime networks
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and limited coastal enforcement create openings for narcotics trafficking, illegal fishing, and external criminal networks to challenge state sovereignty.

highlights: Regional logistics hub remains strategically valuable

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked fiscal reforms and substantial Chinese lending continue to narrow Nairobi's room for maneuver. Control over major transport and energy projects remains politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and the LAPSSET corridor face competition from Tanzanian and Djiboutian routes. Gulf, Chinese, and Western actors are seeking influence over Kenya's logistics and energy networks.

highlights: Water remains the core sovereign asset
Economic dependence on South Africa persists

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa generate vital revenue but leave the kingdom dependent on South African financing, infrastructure, and purchasing arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and labor vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains exposed to external trade preferences and South African supply chains. Factory closures or shifts in foreign sourcing can rapidly weaken employment and fiscal stability.

highlights: Port and road investment attract competing partners

frictionVectors.title: Mining concession asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and other resource agreements provide badly needed revenue but leave Liberia exposed to foreign operators, volatile commodity prices, and disputes over local benefits and environmental safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment in Freeport of Monrovia, roads, and mining corridors is strategically important but can lock infrastructure priorities to concession interests rather than broad national development.

highlights: Oil remains divided by political authority
Foreign security patrons shape national access

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented oil governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and security centers continue to contest control over production, export terminals, and public revenue. Disruptions can be used as leverage in broader power struggles.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military entrenchment
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked networks, and regional actors retain influence through security partnerships and local proxies. Their presence complicates unified border, energy, and infrastructure policy.

highlights: Critical minerals draw intense outside interest

frictionVectors.title: Mining sovereignty and revenue capture
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, graphite, and ilmenite projects bring foreign capital but expose Madagascar to disputes over taxation, environmental damage, community rights, and the distribution of export earnings.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining corridors, ports, and energy systems are often developed around foreign-led projects. Limited domestic infrastructure reduces the state's leverage in negotiating long-term resource contracts.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking foreign capital for uranium, rare-earth and graphite projects while trying to improve state oversight and local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Mozambique Transit Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Fuel and import security remain vulnerable to disruptions on Mozambique-linked transport corridors, constraining Malawi's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is pressing foreign gold operators for larger state shares and tighter compliance, raising the risk of costly disputes and production disruption.

frictionVectors.title: Africa Corps Reliance
frictionVectors.details: Security cooperation with Russia-linked forces has reduced Western leverage but deepened dependence on an external military partner amid persistent insurgency.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Governance
frictionVectors.details: The Senegal-Mauritania offshore gas project offers major fiscal upside, but cross-border revenue management and operator control will test sovereign bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on foreign-led iron-ore investment and export infrastructure leaves Mauritania exposed to commodity cycles and external financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Transition
frictionVectors.details: The sovereignty settlement and future operation of strategic facilities around Chagos remain sensitive to British and American security interests.

frictionVectors.title: External Capital Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius retains strong institutional control, but its port, tourism and financial sectors remain exposed to foreign investment cycles and climate-related shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Contest
frictionVectors.details: Morocco's resource and infrastructure expansion in Western Sahara continues to face diplomatic, legal and regional opposition despite growing external commercial engagement.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Energy Stress
frictionVectors.details: Drought and dependence on imported energy complicate Morocco's industrial ambitions, increasing pressure for desalination, renewables and foreign technology partnerships.

highlights: LNG revival remains central to national recovery
Security gains depend on foreign-backed forces

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence continues to threaten LNG infrastructure and local sovereignty. Mozambique remains dependent on Rwanda and other external security support to protect strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Revenue and Contract Control
frictionVectors.details: International operators and lenders retain major leverage over project financing and commercial terms. Delayed production limits the state's fiscal room and bargaining power.

highlights: Oil and green hydrogen raise strategic leverage
Resource nationalism is being tested by foreign capital

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Recent discoveries could transform Namibia's fiscal position, but foreign majors control much of the capital, technology, and operating capacity. Local-content and revenue-sharing rules will determine how much sovereignty is retained.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Large projects depend on external investors, export corridors, and substantial water and power infrastructure. Land, water allocation, and community-benefit disputes could slow implementation.

highlights: Junta asserts control over strategic resources

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The military government is seeking greater control over uranium and other extractive projects while reducing Western influence. Production, investment, and technical capacity remain vulnerable to diplomatic rupture and regulatory uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Export Corridor
frictionVectors.details: The Niger-Benin export route is strategically important but exposed to political disputes, insurgency, and border tensions. Dependence on external pipeline infrastructure limits Niger's immediate control over monetizing its crude.

highlights: Oil insecurity still drains state capacity

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Pipeline Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Sabotage, theft, and insecurity continue to reduce public revenue and weaken control over producing regions. Foreign operators and private security remain important to maintaining production infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Refining and Gas Investment
frictionVectors.details: New domestic refining capacity improves Nigeria's leverage over fuel supply, but imported equipment, financing, and foreign participation remain significant. Regulatory uncertainty and fiscal pressure could limit the sovereignty gains.

highlights: Strategic autonomy rests on disciplined state capacity
Regional mineral politics threaten diplomatic space

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral Conflict
frictionVectors.details: Allegations of support for armed groups in eastern Congo expose Rwanda to sanctions, diplomatic pressure, and scrutiny over mineral flows. Regional instability also threatens cross-border trade and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Investment Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda maintains strong control over domestic policy but remains reliant on external aid, concessional finance, and foreign investment for infrastructure. Donor criticism can therefore translate into meaningful economic pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Licensing
frictionVectors.details: Exploration in the Gulf of Guinea could strengthen state revenues, but limited regulatory capacity and external operators leave São Tomé exposed to unfavorable terms.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ports, connectivity, and tourism infrastructure rely heavily on foreign finance and partners, constraining independent economic strategy.

highlights: Resource nationalism meets first gas revenues

frictionVectors.title: Oil-and-Gas Contract Review
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater transparency and domestic value from Sangomar oil and GTA gas while avoiding investor flight, arbitration, and production delays.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fishing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fleets and opaque licensing continue to strain coastal livelihoods, complicating Dakar's effort to assert control over marine resources.

highlights: Blue economy remains the sovereignty anchor

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fishing Access
frictionVectors.details: The country retains strong formal control over its maritime zone, but monitoring distant-water fleets and negotiating access remain persistent sovereignty challenges.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Indian, Chinese, European, and Gulf engagement in maritime security and infrastructure offers leverage but requires careful balancing to prevent strategic dependency.

highlights: Energy and transport gaps preserve leverage for outsiders

frictionVectors.title: Iron-Ore Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron-ore and rutile operations generate exports and jobs, but foreign control of capital, logistics, and processing limits Sierra Leone's ability to capture full resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Port-and-Rail Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Mineral corridors and port infrastructure are closely tied to concession holders and external financiers, creating bargaining risks for the government.

highlights: Offshore oil ambitions collide with federal fragmentation
Ports and security partnerships drive sovereignty contest

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Federal licensing plans and foreign exploration interests remain contested by member states, with weak institutions limiting Somalia's ability to secure transparent and nationally accepted terms.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Port Rivalries
frictionVectors.details: Turkish, Gulf, and Ethiopian involvement in security and port access expands external influence while disputes over Somaliland and maritime jurisdiction intensify sovereignty risks.

highlights: Grid and rail recovery remains central

frictionVectors.title: Port, Rail, and Power Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity shortages and logistics constraints limit South Africa's control over mineral value chains. Private-sector participation and reform partnerships are expanding, but they also increase dependence on external capital and expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Critical-Minerals Partners
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, the European Union, and Gulf investors are competing for influence in battery and strategic-mineral supply chains. Pretoria is using this rivalry to preserve policy autonomy, though infrastructure financing remains a vulnerability.

highlights: Oil lifeline exposed to Sudan war

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Export Dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil revenue depends on export infrastructure crossing war-affected Sudan, leaving production and fiscal survival vulnerable to external conflict. Foreign operators and transit authorities retain substantial leverage over the country's resource income.

frictionVectors.title: Armed Competition Over Oil Regions
frictionVectors.details: Political and militia rivalries around oil-producing areas threaten production, worker safety, and revenue allocation. Weak institutions limit Juba's ability to convert resource wealth into sovereign development.

highlights: War fragments control of gold and ports

frictionVectors.title: Gold Networks and Armed Finance
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling remain critical revenue sources for competing armed actors, with regional and international intermediaries shaping access to markets. This weakens civilian sovereignty and sustains the conflict economy.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The Red Sea coast, Port Sudan, and transport corridors attract competing Gulf, Russian, Egyptian, and other external interests. Infrastructure and security partnerships risk becoming instruments of wartime influence rather than national reconstruction.

highlights: LNG and rail projects expand strategic leverage
Mineral policy seeks greater local capture

frictionVectors.title: LNG Bargaining and Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Planned gas development could strengthen Tanzania's fiscal and energy position, but foreign operators and lenders will shape project terms, timelines, and export exposure. Dar es Salaam is balancing commercial partners to avoid excessive dependence on any single bloc.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals and Local Processing
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is tightening expectations for domestic beneficiation and state participation in strategic minerals. Enforcement capacity and competition among Chinese, Western, Gulf, and regional investors remain decisive.

highlights: Lomé port remains a regional power asset

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé gives Togo influence over Sahel trade, but its revenues and strategic importance depend heavily on neighboring states and foreign shipping, logistics, and security partners. Disruptions in Burkina Faso and northern Benin could weaken corridor sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate and External Investment
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate and logistics development attract outside capital while the government seeks greater domestic control and value addition. Limited industrial capacity constrains Togo's ability to retain more resource rents.

highlights: EU Leverage Over Migration and Energy

frictionVectors.title: European Migration Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European financial and political support is increasingly tied to Tunisia's role in stopping irregular migration, narrowing its policy autonomy. The arrangement creates leverage over domestic security and border infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on imported hydrocarbons and constrained electricity interconnections exposes Tunisia to external price and supply shocks. Delays in renewables and grid investment limit near-term sovereign energy control.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to Kampala's resource strategy but faces environmental opposition, financing constraints, and external political pressure. Delays could increase dependence on foreign operators and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Backed Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign contractors remain important to roads, energy, and industrial projects, while debt-service obligations constrain fiscal room. Uganda retains formal ownership but has limited bargaining power over project terms.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Copper Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater local processing, tax capture, and transparency from multinational copper investors, but foreign firms still dominate capital, technology, and export logistics. Competition among Chinese, Gulf, and Western investors gives Lusaka more options without eliminating dependency.

frictionVectors.title: Hydropower and Grid Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Low water levels and underinvestment have exposed Zambia's dependence on hydropower and regional electricity imports. Power shortages directly constrain mining expansion and weaken the government's negotiating position with external investors.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Dominance in Critical Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Zimbabwe has imposed measures intended to encourage domestic mineral processing, but Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in lithium and other strategic-mineral projects. Limited financing alternatives reduce Harare's ability to dictate terms or retain value locally.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions, Currency, and Energy Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions exposure, monetary instability, and unreliable electricity raise the cost of sovereign industrial policy. These pressures increase dependence on foreign investors and neighboring states for capital, fuel, and power.
